assessment.nobel_worthiness: Car-Parrinello ab initio molecular dynamics joined density-functional electronic structure with atomic motion in a single scheme, making finite-temperature, disordered and reacting systems tractable from first principles. It is original, clear in concept and has reshaped computational condensed-matter physics, chemistry and materials science for four decades. From my own field I regard its lasting impact as exceptional, while recognizing that the computational-method character is a matter on which the committee may weigh physics content against tool-building.
assessment.attribution: The 1985 paper by Car and Parrinello is the unambiguous origin and the two names cleanly define a two-person prize. Later extensions (Born-Oppenheimer variants, path-integral and metadynamics-related work) involve others but are not the core discovery.
assessment.maturity: Forty years of near-universal use and independent validation; recognition is, if anything, overdue. The Kohn chemistry prize of 1998 recognized DFT itself, and this builds on it rather than duplicating it.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views a simulation method as a physics discovery or as instrumentation of the kind it has been reluctant to honor.
Overlap in perception with the 1998 chemistry prize for density-functional theory.
I rely on my own recollection of the history and have not independently verified details of priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators opened a new class of matter in which band topology and spin-orbit coupling give protected edge and surface states. The idea is conceptually deep, clearly formulated, and has had broad influence across electronic-structure theory, spintronics and quantum materials. Electronic-structure calculations were also decisive in identifying real materials, which I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the theoretical formulation; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental demonstration in HgTe quantum wells. The supplied credit supports a natural theory-plus-experiment trio. Other contributors such as Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (HgTe prediction), Fu, Moore and Balents, and Hasan, are not among the credited names, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by many independent experiments (HgTe, Bi-based compounds, ARPES, transport), and the interpretation is stable. Timing is good, though the Nobel 2016 topological-phase prize partly overlaps in conceptual territory.
uncertainties: Disputed credit between the theory and experimental communities and among several prediction groups.
Partial conceptual overlap with the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases.
Practical applications remain limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the subsequent discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene created the moire quantum-matter field. The surprise that a tunable twist controls strongly correlated physics in a clean carbon system fits the theme that quantum mechanics keeps offering new surprises. It is original and has had remarkable breadth in just several years.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction (2011); Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery with Cao and collaborators. The credited trio is a coherent prediction-plus-discovery configuration, though the first experimental author, Yuan Cao, and others such as Dean, Young and Yazdani contributed to the experimental understanding and are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories, but the nature of the superconducting pairing and correlated phases is still debated. Recognition may be somewhat early, though the foundational prediction and discovery are secure.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and correlated states is unresolved.
Experimental credit beyond the senior author is not represented, and sample-quality dependence persists.
Possible prematurity compared with more settled candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's demonstration of record accuracy and coherence, brought fractional uncertainties to the 10^-18 level and enabled tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. The idea is elegant and the impact on metrology is large and clearly articulated. It lies outside my specialty, so I judge it on clarity and impact.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first realized the lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping; Ye led the highest-precision realizations and many-body clock work. A two-person prize is a clean allocation. Hall and Hansch received the 2005 prize for the frequency comb, which was an enabling technology, and ion-clock work by Wineland (2012) is related but distinct.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many national metrology laboratories and by direct clock comparisons. Redefinition of the second is under discussion, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Possible overlap in the committee's mind with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Other contributors such as Lemonde, Takamoto or Derevianko are not credited.
I have not verified the current record uncertainties independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Using ultracold atoms in optical lattices as programmable analogue simulators of Hubbard-type models, this work realized the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and extended to strongly correlated many-body physics. For someone who computes correlated lattice models, a tunable laboratory realization with single-site resolution is of great importance, even if quantitative simulation of the hardest problems remains an open goal.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) proposed the Hubbard-model realization; Greiner and Bloch carried out the 2002 Mott-insulator experiment and quantum gas microscopes. Esslinger's fermionic work is also relevant and a fourth credited person, so any three-person limit leaves out important contributors; Jaksch is not credited at all.
assessment.maturity: Mature and replicated worldwide; however, the question of whether it has delivered decisive new insight into open problems such as high-temperature superconductivity continues.
uncertainties: Choosing three of four credited names is an arbitrary-looking trade-off, and Jaksch and others are missing.
Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 atomic-physics prizes.
Scientific payoff for open correlated-electron problems is still limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The spin Hall effect, in which a charge current generates a transverse spin current through spin-orbit coupling, is a fundamental transport phenomenon underlying spin-orbit torques and modern spintronics. It connects directly to the magnetism and spin dynamics that I know well, and its relevance to magnetization switching in memory devices is substantial.
assessment.attribution: Dyakonov and Perel made the 1971 prediction; Awschalom's group (Kato et al.) observed it optically in 2004 and Jungwirth with collaborators the electrical observation in 2005. Perel died in 2002 and is not eligible and not credited, and Hirsch, Zhang, Sinova and others are involved in the intrinsic-effect theory and the revival. The suggested trio is plausible but credit is complicated.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and exploited in devices, with the inverse and anomalous variants also established. Interpretation is stable though extrinsic and intrinsic contributions remain material-dependent.
uncertainties: Complicated credit: an eligible laureate set omits the deceased co-predictor and other theorists.
Overlap with the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize in the spintronics area.
Some branch effects such as the quantum spin Hall variant are covered elsewhere.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in iron pnictides and chalcogenides, with Tc up to 55 K in bulk samples, established a second family of high-temperature superconductors with magnetism intertwined with pairing. It is a significant discovery, and as a magnetism and electronic-structure theorist I find the interplay of spin fluctuations, orbital physics and correlations especially instructive.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's 2008 LaFeAsO(F) report is the decisive discovery; Chen and Zhao rapidly raised Tc via rare-earth substitution in the same weeks. Other groups (such as Wen, Wang) also contributed. The credit is workable with Hosono central, though the order and the role of secondary discoverers is open to dispute.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently and extensively, with a stable experimental picture. The microscopic pairing mechanism is not settled, and practical conductors are only developing.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism remains debated.
Competing or additional claims of priority in the raising of Tc.
The cuprate prize of 1987 may make the committee view this as incremental.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical addressing and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, with room-temperature spin readout, created a versatile platform for nanoscale magnetometry, thermometry and quantum information. It is important and has a wide range of uses, including imaging of magnetic textures that I find relevant.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup (with Gruber and colleagues) detected single NV centers optically in 1997 and Jelezko demonstrated coherent control; Lukin's group advanced the quantum-register and sensing work. Other important contributors, such as Awschalom, Hanson, Walsworth, Maze and Yacoby, are not credited, so the allocation is not clean.
assessment.maturity: Replicated broadly and mature as a technique; the sensing applications are still developing, so the recognition might be reasonable but not urgent.
uncertainties: The decisive credit among many leading NV groups is ambiguous.
Whether the core discovery is the physics or the application to sensing.
I have not independently verified priority dates.
